The Roman Empire, one of the most influential and powerful civilizations in human history, has a rich and complex past that spans over 12 centuries. The story of Rome begins in 753 BC, when the city was founded by Romulus and Remus, two legendary brothers who are said to have been raised by a she-wolf. According to myth, Romulus became the first king of Rome, marking the beginning of the Roman Kingdom.

During the Roman Kingdom (753 BC - 509 BC), Rome was ruled by seven kings, each contributing to the growth and development of the city. The kingdom was characterized by a system of governance in which the king held absolute power, but was also advised by a council of elders known as the Senate. This period saw the construction of key infrastructure, including the Roman Forum, the heart of the city, and the establishment of trade relationships with neighboring cities.

As the Roman Kingdom progressed, tensions arose between the ruling class and the common people, ultimately leading to the expulsion of the last king, Lucius Tarquinius Superbus, in 509 BC. This event marked the end of the Roman Kingdom and the beginning of the Roman Republic (509 BC - 27 BC), a system of government in which power was held by the people and their elected representatives. The Roman Republic was characterized by a system of governance in which two consuls, elected annually, held executive power, and the Senate advised on matters of state.

The early years of the Roman Republic were marked by conflict with neighboring cities and states, including the Etruscans and the Latins. However, through a series of military victories and strategic alliances, Rome was able to expand its territories and establish itself as a dominant force in the region.
